title: Gestational Diabetes: Glucose Control and Newborn Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Gestational diabetes increases risks such as fetal overgrowth, hypertensive disorders, birth complications, and neonatal hypoglycemia. Care centers on glucose monitoring, nutrition/activity, medication when needed, fetal surveillance as indicated, and postpartum diabetes testing because maternal future type 2 diabetes risk remains elevated.
recognize: Gestational diabetes is often asymptomatic and is usually found through routine pregnancy screening.
Poor glycemic control can contribute to macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, polyhydramnios, preeclampsia, and neonatal metabolic complications.
Insulin resistance falls rapidly after placental delivery, so medication needs can change immediately postpartum.
priorities: Monitor glucose according to the obstetric plan and report persistent values outside targets.
Assess nutrition access, medication technique, fetal-movement concerns, and hypoglycemia risk.
Prepare for newborn glucose monitoring when indicated after birth.
assessMonitor: Trend fasting/post-meal glucose as prescribed, fetal growth/surveillance when ordered, blood pressure, maternal weight/nutrition, and medication adverse effects.
interventions: Reinforce individualized meal planning and safe pregnancy activity.
Administer insulin or other pregnancy-appropriate therapy exactly as ordered.
Ensure postpartum glucose testing and long-term primary-care follow-up are included in discharge planning.
medicationSafety: Insulin can cause hypoglycemia; match dosing with food intake and glucose plan.
Pregnancy medication choices are clinician-directed and should not be extrapolated from routine nonpregnant diabetes care.
teaching: Gestational diabetes usually improves after delivery but future diabetes risk persists; postpartum testing and ongoing screening matter.
delegationScope: Routine glucose checks may be delegated where policy permits; interpretation of abnormal trends and pregnancy complications requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming diabetes follow-up ends when the placenta is delivered.
oneLinePearl: GDM is pregnancy-limited glucose intolerance with lifelong follow-up implications.
sourceBasis: ACOG Practice Bulletin 190: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus, reaffirmed 2024
American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

title: Placenta Previa vs Abruption
bottomLine: Late-pregnancy bleeding is an obstetric emergency until evaluated. Placenta previa classically causes painless bright-red bleeding; placental abruption more often causes painful bleeding with uterine tenderness or rigidity and may be concealed. Do not perform a digital vaginal examination when placenta previa has not been excluded.
recognize: Previa bleeding is often painless and recurrent.
Abruption may cause abdominal/back pain, uterine tenderness, frequent contractions, fetal distress, and bleeding that can be less visible than the true blood loss.
Abruption risk increases with hypertension, trauma, smoking/cocaine exposure, and prior abruption.
priorities: Assess ABCs, maternal vital signs/perfusion, amount/color of bleeding, pain, uterine tone, and fetal status.
Establish/maintain IV access and prepare blood work/products as ordered for significant bleeding.
Avoid digital vaginal examination until placental location is known when previa is possible.
assessMonitor: Trend maternal hemodynamics, fetal heart pattern, contractions, bleeding, urine output, CBC/coagulation data when ordered, and signs of DIC.
interventions: Position to optimize maternal-fetal perfusion and administer oxygen only when clinically indicated for maternal hypoxemia/distress according to the obstetric emergency plan.
Prepare for urgent delivery when maternal or fetal instability requires it.
medicationSafety: Rh-negative unsensitized patients with bleeding may require Rh immune globulin according to gestational age and protocol.
Tocolysis is not a routine response to significant abruption and requires obstetric direction.
teaching: Any significant pregnancy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, or decreased fetal movement needs urgent evaluation.
delegationScope: Acute pregnancy bleeding requires licensed-nurse assessment and immediate obstetric escalation; do not delegate initial evaluation.
examTrap: Performing a digital cervical examination for painless third-trimester bleeding before placenta previa is excluded.
oneLinePearl: Previa is usually painless; abruption hurts—but both can bleed dangerously.

title: Preterm Labor and PPROM: Infection, Cord, and Lung Maturity
bottomLine: Regular contractions, pelvic pressure, backache, discharge change, or ruptured membranes before 37 weeks require prompt obstetric evaluation. With PPROM, priorities include fetal status, infection, cord prolapse, gestational age, and balancing the risks of prematurity against continuing the pregnancy.
recognize: PPROM may present as a gush or persistent trickle of fluid before labor.
Fever, uterine tenderness, maternal/fetal tachycardia, or foul fluid can suggest intraamniotic infection.
Sudden fetal bradycardia after membrane rupture raises concern for cord prolapse.
priorities: Assess contractions, gestational age, fluid loss, fever, uterine tenderness, fetal movement, and fetal heart pattern.
Avoid unnecessary digital vaginal examinations after membrane rupture because they can increase infection risk and shorten latency.
Escalate cord prolapse, infection, significant bleeding, or nonreassuring fetal status immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend maternal temperature, pulse, uterine tenderness, fetal heart pattern, contractions, fluid characteristics, and ordered labs.
interventions: Administer antenatal corticosteroids, latency antibiotics, magnesium for fetal neuroprotection, or tocolysis only when ordered and gestationally appropriate.
Maintain pelvic rest and other precautions according to the obstetric plan.
medicationSafety: Tocolytics are used selectively and are not appropriate when delivery is required for infection, severe bleeding, or major maternal/fetal compromise.
Medication timing depends heavily on gestational age and local protocol.
teaching: Call promptly for contractions, fluid leakage, bleeding, fever, or decreased fetal movement before term.
delegationScope: PPROM/preterm labor assessment and fetal-status interpretation require licensed obstetric nursing evaluation; LPN/LVN participation follows state/facility scope.
examTrap: Performing repeated digital vaginal examinations after PPROM to check progress when infection risk is a concern.
oneLinePearl: PPROM means watch infection, cord, bleeding, and fetal status—not just contractions.
sourceBasis: ACOG Practice Bulletin 217: Prelabor Rupture of Membranes, reaffirmed 2023 with 2025 advisory
ACOG Preterm Labor and Birth Guidance

title: Fetal Heart Decelerations: Find the Cause, Fix Perfusion
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Fetal heart patterns are interpreted in context, not by memorizing one maneuver. Early decelerations usually mirror head compression; variable decelerations suggest cord compression; recurrent late decelerations suggest impaired uteroplacental oxygen transfer and require intrauterine resuscitative measures plus escalation if they persist.
recognize: Early decelerations generally begin and recover with contractions.
Variable decelerations are abrupt and vary in timing/shape.
Late decelerations begin after the contraction starts and recover after the contraction ends; absent/minimal variability or bradycardia increases concern.
priorities: Reposition the patient to improve uteroplacental perfusion, commonly lateral positioning.
Stop or reduce uterotonic stimulation such as oxytocin when ordered/protocol indicates tachysystole or recurrent concerning patterns.
Assess maternal BP/oxygenation, contraction frequency, and fetal variability and escalate persistent Category II deterioration or Category III patterns promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend baseline rate, variability, accelerations/decelerations, contraction frequency, maternal blood pressure, temperature, and response to interventions.
interventions: Correct maternal hypotension and excessive uterine activity according to orders/protocol.
Prepare for expedited delivery if an abnormal pattern does not resolve and obstetric assessment indicates it.
medicationSafety: Oxytocin can cause uterine tachysystole and fetal compromise; infusion management authority varies by state/facility for LPN/LVN practice.
Routine maternal oxygen solely for an abnormal fetal tracing when the mother is normoxemic is not a universal first-line intervention; follow current obstetric protocol.
redFlags: Recurrent late decelerations with absent variability
teaching: Explain position changes and monitoring interventions briefly while maintaining urgent maternal-fetal care.
delegationScope: Interpretation and management of fetal heart patterns require licensed obstetric nursing competency and facility-defined scope.
examTrap: Treating every deceleration with the same intervention without considering timing, variability, contractions, and maternal status.
oneLinePearl: Early=head, variable=cord, late=placenta—then assess the whole tracing.
sourceBasis: ACOG 2025 Clinical Practice Guideline: Intrapartum Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring
ACOG Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring resources

title: RSV Bronchiolitis: Work of Breathing and Hydration
bottomLine: RSV bronchiolitis is usually managed with supportive care. The nursing danger signs are apnea, increasing retractions/work of breathing, cyanosis/hypoxemia, exhaustion, and poor feeding with dehydration; young infants may have little or no fever.
recognize: Runny nose, cough, wheeze/crackles, tachypnea, retractions, and reduced feeding can develop over several days.
Very young infants may present mainly with irritability, decreased activity, poor intake, or apnea.
Prematurity, chronic lung disease, significant congenital heart disease, immune compromise, or young age increase severe-disease risk.
priorities: Assess respiratory rate/effort, retractions, nasal flaring, apnea, oxygenation, hydration, feeding tolerance, and fatigue.
Suction nasal secretions gently when they impair feeding or breathing.
Provide oxygen and hydration support when clinically indicated and escalate worsening respiratory failure.
assessMonitor: Trend work of breathing, oxygenation, apnea, intake/output, wet diapers, and ability to feed safely.
interventions: Use small frequent feeds only when respiratory effort allows safe feeding; use IV/enteral support when ordered if intake is inadequate.
Follow current infection-control precautions for respiratory viruses.
medicationSafety: Routine antibiotics do not treat RSV.
Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, or nebulized therapies are not routine for every bronchiolitis patient and should be used only when specifically indicated/ordered.
redFlags: Poor intake with few wet diapers
teaching: Seek care for difficulty breathing, worsening symptoms, or inadequate fluid intake; discuss RSV immunization prevention options with the pediatric clinician.
delegationScope: Routine diaper counts may be delegated, but changing respiratory effort or apnea requires immediate licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Waiting for fever before recognizing severe RSV in a young infant with apnea and poor feeding.
oneLinePearl: In infant RSV, breathing and feeding tell you severity better than fever.
sourceBasis: CDC 2026 RSV Symptoms and Care Guidance
CDC RSV Immunization Guidance for Infants and Young Children

title: Pyloric Stenosis: Projectile Vomiting and Alkalosis
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically causes progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting in a young infant who may remain hungry after vomiting. Repeated gastric acid loss causes dehydration and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis; correct fluids/electrolytes before pyloromyotomy.
recognize: Vomiting is nonbilious because obstruction is proximal to the duodenum.
Weight loss/poor gain, fewer wet diapers, visible gastric peristalsis, and an olive-like RUQ/epigastric mass may occur.
Bilious vomiting points away from pyloric stenosis and toward a more distal obstruction that can be emergent.
priorities: Assess hydration, weight trend, urine output, emesis color, electrolytes, and acid-base status.
Keep NPO and begin ordered IV fluid/electrolyte correction.
Escalate bilious emesis, shock, severe lethargy, or marked electrolyte disturbance.
assessMonitor: Trend chloride, potassium, bicarbonate, weight, urine output, and response to rehydration.
interventions: Prepare for surgical pyloromyotomy after metabolic stabilization.
Provide postoperative feeding progression according to the surgical plan.
medicationSafety: Do not treat ongoing projectile vomiting solely with antiemetics while obstruction remains uncorrected.
Electrolyte correction should follow pediatric orders to avoid rapid shifts.
teaching: Parents should seek care for repeated forceful vomiting, poor urine output, or weight loss in a young infant.
delegationScope: Intake/output measurement may be delegated; emesis characterization and dehydration assessment require licensed-nurse evaluation.
examTrap: Assuming projectile vomiting in a young infant is uncomplicated reflux.
oneLinePearl: Pyloric stenosis = hungry baby, nonbilious projectile vomit, dehydration, alkalosis.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Pediatrics pediatric surgical care principles
American College of Radiology pediatric vomiting criteria

title: Intussusception: Episodic Pain, Lethargy, and Ischemia
bottomLine: Intussusception is telescoping of bowel that can obstruct blood flow. Sudden episodic severe abdominal pain with drawing up of the legs, vomiting, lethargy, and later bloody or currant-jelly stool requires urgent evaluation; the classic stool is a late finding and should not be awaited.
recognize: Children may appear well between painful episodes early in the course.
Lethargy can be prominent and may be mistaken for a primary neurologic illness.
A sausage-shaped abdominal mass may be present, but absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
priorities: Assess pain episodes, hydration, emesis color, stool, abdominal distention/tenderness, perfusion, and mental status.
Keep NPO and establish ordered IV support.
Escalate peritoneal signs, shock, bilious vomiting, or perforation concern immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend vital signs, abdominal findings, stool, intake/output, pain pattern, and response after reduction.
interventions: Prepare for ultrasound and air/contrast enema reduction when appropriate.
Prepare for surgery if nonoperative reduction fails or perforation/peritonitis is present.
medicationSafety: Analgesia should not be withheld solely to preserve diagnostic signs.
Laxatives or enemas for constipation should not be given outside the diagnostic reduction plan when obstruction is suspected.
teaching: Recurrent episodic pain, lethargy, vomiting, or blood/mucus in stool needs urgent pediatric evaluation.
delegationScope: Acute abdominal pain assessment is a licensed-nurse responsibility; routine output tracking may be delegated with reporting thresholds.
examTrap: Waiting for currant-jelly stool before escalating an infant with episodic screaming, leg flexion, vomiting, and lethargy.
oneLinePearl: Intussusception comes in waves; blood in the stool may come late.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Pediatrics pediatric emergency principles
American College of Radiology pediatric intussusception criteria

title: Kawasaki Disease: Fever and Coronary Risk
bottomLine: Kawasaki disease is an acute childhood vasculitis in which delayed treatment increases coronary-artery complication risk. Persistent fever with compatible mucocutaneous findings should trigger prompt pediatric evaluation even when every classic feature is not present, especially in young infants.
recognize: Features can include prolonged fever, bilateral nonpurulent conjunctival injection, oral/lip changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, and cervical lymphadenopathy.
Incomplete Kawasaki disease occurs, particularly in infants.
Coronary artery dilation/aneurysm is the major feared complication.
priorities: Assess fever duration, hydration, irritability, mucocutaneous findings, cardiac symptoms, and perfusion.
Escalate promptly for diagnostic evaluation and echocardiography when Kawasaki disease is suspected.
Administer IVIG and aspirin therapy as ordered and monitor response.
assessMonitor: Trend fever, inflammatory markers when ordered, cardiac status, and echocardiographic follow-up.
Monitor for recurrent fever after IVIG and signs of coronary complications.
interventions: Provide comfort, hydration, and mouth/skin care.
Coordinate cardiology follow-up when coronary involvement is present.
medicationSafety: Aspirin is usually avoided in viral illnesses in children because of Reye syndrome risk, but Kawasaki disease is a specific clinician-directed exception.
Live-virus vaccine timing may need adjustment after IVIG; follow immunization guidance.
teaching: Keep all cardiology and echocardiography follow-up; coronary risk can persist beyond the acute fever.
delegationScope: Recognition of the febrile mucocutaneous pattern and cardiac changes requires licensed-nurse assessment and prompt pediatric escalation.
examTrap: Rejecting Kawasaki disease because the child has only four classic features despite prolonged fever and supportive findings.
oneLinePearl: Persistent fever plus mucocutaneous inflammation means protect the coronaries early.
sourceBasis: American Heart Association 2024 Update on Diagnosis and Management of Kawasaki Disease

title: Cyanotic Tet Spell: Calm, Knees Up, Escalate
bottomLine: A hypercyanotic or tet spell in a child with Tetralogy of Fallot is an acute drop in pulmonary blood flow. Keep the child calm, place in a knee-chest/squatting-type position as age allows, provide ordered oxygen/supportive care, and escalate immediately if cyanosis or distress persists.
recognize: Episodes may be triggered by crying, feeding, defecation, dehydration, or exertion.
The child may become suddenly deeply cyanotic, tachypneic, irritable, weak, or syncopal.
Older children may instinctively squat because increasing systemic vascular resistance can improve pulmonary blood flow.
priorities: Keep the child calm and minimize agitation.
Use knee-chest positioning in infants or allow squatting in older children when appropriate.
Assess airway/breathing, oxygenation, perfusion, and mental status and activate pediatric emergency response.
assessMonitor: Trend color, oxygenation, respiratory effort, heart rate, level of consciousness, hydration, and response to positioning/therapy.
interventions: Administer oxygen and prescribed medications/fluids under emergency orders.
Prepare for advanced pediatric cardiac management if the spell does not resolve.
medicationSafety: Morphine, beta blockade, or vasoconstrictor therapy may be used in monitored settings under clinician direction; these are not independent PN treatment decisions.
teaching: Caregivers of children with known Tetralogy of Fallot should know the emergency positioning and when to call EMS.
delegationScope: Acute cyanosis is not a delegated assessment; initiate immediate licensed nursing response and escalation.
examTrap: Forcing a screaming cyanotic toddler flat in bed instead of reducing agitation and using knee-chest/squatting positioning.
oneLinePearl: Tet spell: calm child, knees up, oxygen/support, call for help.
sourceBasis: American Heart Association congenital heart disease resources
